name: Uradhi, Atampaya dialect
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 1983. Uradhi. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds.), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 3, 306-428. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins. (ANU Open Research digitisation hdl:1885/114846)
catalog_locator: section 2.3 'Stress', p.322 (PDF page 344); vowel length p.318 (section 2.1)
catalog_quote: 2.3 STRESS The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' /íku/ 'bandicoot' /íntinu/ 'story-place of brown snake' /túyuβa/ 'cigarette' /umúyanu/ 'nose' /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.) The following examples (again from the Atampaya dialect) are chosen to illustrate this: /ití:na/ 'thigh'…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page image we hold and text layer of Crowley 1983 p.322 (PDF p.344), section 2.3 'Stress'; the vowel-length locator p.318 also checks out and adds a refinement already consistent with the classification (underived long vowels confined to the first two syllables; lengthening suffixes such as genitive /-:namu/ create later long vowels, hence /tá:rá:namu/ with two primaries). (2) The deciding source is the HAL grammar sketch by the language's principal fieldworker, the fullest description that exists; Glottolog lists no later grammar, phonology or instrumental work and marks Uradhi extinct. (3) The one unheld item that bears on this record is Hale 1976 (AIAS print volume, not open), relevant only to explaining the StressTyp2/WALS 'second syllable' discrepancy, not to the classification itself; Crowley 1980 (PL A-59) was downloaded from the open PL archive and is silent on stres

sources.quote: None. The paper treats Atampaya/Angkamuthi/Yadhaykenu word-boundary sandhi and syllable-structure targets; the only prosodic-adjacent remark is that Angkamuthi has underlying final long vowels derived historically from -Vl sequences (p.252). No statement on stress placement.

sources.note: The only other Glottolog phonology reference for Uradhi and one of the two sources StressTyp2 lists for its Uradhi entry (seen in our StressTyp2 SQL dump); StressTyp2/WALS code Uradhi as second-syllable fixed stress, which contradicts Crowley 1983 p.322. Reading Hale's 9 pages would show whether the database 'peninitial' coding reflects a diachronic stress-shift hypothesis for Northern Paman or a competing synchronic statement, and let the record's 'contra' note name the origin of the discrepancy.
